questions.explanation: A direct object is accusative; masculine der becomes den.
mit always takes dative; masculine der becomes dem.
Movement toward a destination takes accusative; feminine die stays die.
hints: The gender of Apotheke (pharmacy) is feminine.
This sentence uses the accusative case because it describes movement toward a destination.
In the accusative case, feminine definite articles stay die.

questions.explanation: A fixed location takes dative; feminine die becomes der.
The recipient is the indirect object, so Frau is dative.
Museum is a neuter direct object; das remains das in accusative.
mit takes dative; plural uses den and usually adds -n to the noun.
Nominative masculine uses the base ein-word form: dein.

questions.prompt: Which case normally marks the direct object?
questions.explanation: The accusative case marks the direct object.

questions.prompt: Which case normally marks the indirect object?
questions.explanation: The dative case commonly marks the recipient or beneficiary.

questions.prompt: durch, ohne, gegen, für, um take which case?
questions.explanation: The DOGFU prepositions always take accusative.

questions.prompt: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu take which case?
questions.explanation: These common prepositions always take dative.
Two-way prepositions take accusative for wohin?—where to?
Two-way prepositions take dative for wo?—where?
ich → mich in the accusative.
er → ihn in the accusative.
ich → mir in the dative.
du → dir in the dative.
sie → ihr means to/for her.
bei dem → beim.
von dem → vom.
zu dem → zum.
zu der → zur.
Es gibt takes accusative; masculine ein becomes einen.
nach is used with cities and countries that have no article.
Countries without an article take nach, not zu.
Home uses the fixed phrase nach Hause.
Directions such as Norden, Süden, Osten, Westen take nach.
Going to a person uses zu (+ dative). zu dem contracts to zum.
zu + dem → zum. People and institutions use zu, not nach.
zu + der → zur. Buildings and institutions take zu.

questions.prompt: Das Geschenk ist für ___ Frau. (die Frau)

questions.prompt: Das Spiel ist gegen ___ Verein. (der Verein)

um always takes accusative; masculine der becomes den.

questions.prompt: Ich lerne Deutsch, ___ in Berlin zu arbeiten.
questions.explanation: Purpose (“in order to”) is um … zu. um comes first; zu sits right before the infinitive.
hints: This clause states a purpose: in order to work in Berlin.
The pattern is um + rest of the clause + zu + infinitive.

questions.prompt: Ich gehe einkaufen, um Brot ___ kaufen.
questions.explanation: zu comes immediately before the infinitive: um Brot zu kaufen.
hints: um … zu wraps the whole purpose clause.
zu is not at the start; it stands right before kaufen.

questions.prompt: Wir fahren nach Berlin, ___ das Museum zu besuchen.
questions.explanation: um introduces the purpose; zu remains in front of besuchen.

questions.prompt: Ich spare Geld, um ein Auto ___ kaufen.
questions.explanation: Objects stay between um and zu: um ein Auto zu kaufen.
um + (complements) + zu + infinitive expresses purpose: in order to.

questions.prompt: “In order to” with no new subject uses…
questions.explanation: Same subject as the main clause: Ich lerne, um zu arbeiten. A different subject needs damit instead.
With separable verbs, zu slots between prefix and stem: anzurufen, not zu anrufen.

With je, parler becomes je parle.
With nous, parler becomes nous parlons.
The first-person form of prendre is prends.
The nous form of aller is allons.
The first-person form of être is suis.
The third-person plural form of être is sont.
The first-person form of avoir is ai.
The vous form of avoir is avez.
nous = we.

questions.prompt: Which subject pronoun means informal singular “you”?
questions.explanation: tu is informal singular you.

questions.prompt: Which subject pronoun means formal or plural “you”?

de + le contracts to du.
à + le contracts to au.
